overlap.title: Naaman and Ard: sons of Benjamin, or sons of Bela?
overlap.summary: Genesis in the KJV lists ten sons of Benjamin, among them Naaman and Ard. Numbers calls Ard and Naaman sons of Bela, Benjamin’s son. Brenton’s Greek of Genesis gives Benjamin three sons and makes the rest sons of Bala and one a son of Gera.
overlap.reasoning: In the KJV of Genesis, Naaman and Ard stand in a list headed “the sons of Benjamin”. In the KJV of Numbers they are sons of Bela, and so Benjamin’s grandsons. The KJV follows the Hebrew in both books. Brenton’s Greek of Genesis divides the list: three sons of Benjamin, five sons of Bala including Noeman, and Arad as a son of Gera. It names nine men where the KJV names ten, and it agrees with Numbers that Noeman is Bala’s son.
overlap.scope: G applies at Genesis 46:21, where the Greek differs from the KJV. The two KJV verses can be reconciled if “sons” in Genesis takes in grandsons, or if there were two men of each name; Genesis says neither. Whether Arad in the Greek of Genesis and Adar in the Greek of Numbers are the same name is not settled here. The total of persons in Genesis 46 is not examined in this record. The supplied KJV source prints “Ard” at Numbers 26:40; the packaged verse and this quotation were corrected together to match it. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

overlap.title: Saul “reigned one year”, or was “a year old” when he began to reign?
overlap.summary: The KJV says “Saul reigned one year”. The Hebrew uses the usual formula for a king’s age at accession and reads “a son of a year was Saul in his reigning”. Brenton’s Greek Septuagint has no verse 1 at all.
overlap.reasoning: At 2 Samuel 2:10 the KJV renders the formula “son of N years … in his reigning” as the king’s age when he began to reign. At 1 Samuel 13:1 the same formula has the number “a year”, and the KJV renders it instead as a length of reign, “reigned one year”. The Hebrew as it stands gives an age, not a length of reign. The named Greek edition omits the verse.
overlap.scope: This is a finding about what the Hebrew words say, not about Saul’s real age: an age of one year cannot be meant as history, and the Hebrew text may have lost a number, but which number is not established here. The KJV wording avoids that difficulty rather than translating the formula as it does elsewhere. G is tagged only because the named Greek edition lacks the verse. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text, with the consonants-only Aleppo-based edition as a second witness. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined, and the KJV translators’ source for their wording is not established here. English glosses in brackets are the researcher’s plain renderings, not lexicon entries. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint; other Greek witnesses were not examined.

overlap.title: “Bring me up Samuel” — by what means did Samuel come up at Endor, and why did the woman cry out?
overlap.summary: The Lord does not answer Saul “by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets”. Saul then asks a woman “that hath a familiar spirit” to bring up Samuel, who is dead. The next sentence says the woman “saw Samuel” and “cried with a loud voice”, and the passage goes on to give words of Samuel that speak in the name of the Lord. The verses compared do not say what the woman did, by whose act Samuel came up, or why she cried out.
overlap.reasoning: The passage sets two things side by side. The laws quoted forbid consulting one “that hath a familiar spirit”, and 28:6 says the Lord would not answer Saul by the three means it names. Yet from 28:12 the narrative itself uses the name Samuel for what the woman sees and for the speaker (“the woman saw Samuel”, “Samuel said to Saul”), and the words spoken name the Lord and say what will happen the next day. Between the request at 28:11 and the sight at 28:12 no act of the woman is told. So the verses quoted leave unstated whether Samuel came up through the woman’s practice, apart from it, or in some other way, and they give no reason for her cry or for how she then knew her visitor was Saul. Which of these is taken decides how the passage bears on the laws quoted and on the statement that the Lord did not answer.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the woman’s practice brought Samuel up; that Samuel was sent apart from anything she did, which is offered as the reason for her cry; that what appeared was not Samuel, although the narrative uses his name. Limits: the narrative calls the one seen and the speaker “Samuel” at 28:12, 28:15, 28:16 and 28:20, and nothing in these verses says the appearance was false; only the woman is said to see, Saul asks her what she saw, and “Saul perceived that it was Samuel” follows her description; the woman’s words at 28:13 are her report, and the KJV’s “gods” there stands for a Hebrew word that the KJV elsewhere renders “God”, with a plural participle; 28:15 has Samuel say “to bring me up”, which states that he was brought up and does not say by whom; 1 Chronicles 10:13 in the KJV says Saul asked counsel of one that had a familiar spirit and does not say what answered, while Brenton’s Greek of that verse adds that “Samuel the prophet answered him”, a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding; Brenton’s Greek of 28:14 has “an upright man” where the KJV has “An old man”, and of 28:19 “with you shall fall” where the KJV has “be with me”, both also stated as wording only. Check made: 1 Samuel 28:3 and 28:6–25 were read in the KJV, verses 3 and 6–20 also in the Hebrew and the Greek; a search of the packaged KJV for “familiar spirit” finds Leviticus 19:31, 20:6, 20:27, Deuteronomy 18:11, 1 Samuel 28:3, 28:7, 28:8, 28:9, 2 Kings 21:6, 23:24, 1 Chronicles 10:13, 2 Chronicles 33:6, Isaiah 8:19, 19:3 and 29:4, and a whole-word search for “Endor” finds Joshua 17:11, 1 Samuel 28:7 and Psalms 83:10. Those are word searches and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle by what means Samuel came up. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. overlap.title: Josiah’s death: slain at Megiddo and carried away dead, or brought wounded to Jerusalem, where he died?
overlap.summary: 2 Kings says Pharaoh slew Josiah at Megiddo and his servants carried him dead from there. 2 Chronicles says he was wounded, moved to another chariot and brought to Jerusalem, “and he died”.
overlap.reasoning: Kings places the death at Megiddo and has a dead man carried to Jerusalem. Chronicles has a wounded man speak, be moved, and be brought to Jerusalem, and only then says he died.
overlap.scope: No tag is proposed: the KJV matches the Hebrew in both books, and the Greek agrees in each. Chronicles does not say in so many words where Josiah died; the order of its clauses puts the death after the journey. If the Hebrew word rendered “dead” in Kings is taken as “dying”, the accounts draw closer; the record does not decide that, and verse 29 still says he was put to death at Megiddo. overlap.title: Jehoiakim: “none to sit upon the throne of David”, or his son reigned in his stead?
overlap.summary: Jeremiah says the Lord declared that Jehoiakim would have none to sit on David’s throne. 2 Kings says his son Jehoiachin reigned in his stead, for three months.
overlap.reasoning: The prophecy says no one of Jehoiakim’s would sit on the throne of David. Kings reports that his son did reign in his place in Jerusalem.
overlap.scope: No tag is proposed: the KJV matches the Hebrew in both books, and the Greek agrees. overlap.title: Zedekiah: Jehoiachin’s uncle, his brother, or his son?
overlap.summary: 2 Kings calls the new king Jehoiachin’s father’s brother. 2 Chronicles calls him Jehoiachin’s brother. The Greek of Kings says “his son”, and the Greek of Chronicles says “his father’s brother”.
overlap.reasoning: The KJV follows the Hebrew in each book and so gives the same man two relationships to Jehoiachin: uncle in Kings, brother in Chronicles. Brenton’s Greek differs from the KJV in both places. In Kings it has “his son”; in Chronicles it has “brother of his father”, which is what the KJV has in Kings.
